headline: Hadley man pleads guilty to importing Russian plutonium and mailing hazardous materials
dek: Jacob D. Miller admitted importing plutonium and selling it through a South Hadley business; federal prosecutors say about 67 plutonium customers and 71 thallium customers received shipments before his arrest.
body: A 44-year-old Massachusetts man has pleaded guilty to importing plutonium from Russia and sending radioactive and toxic materials through the mail from a business run out of his South Hadley home. The plea, announced by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts, adds a new legal milestone to a case that began with a federal search and arrest in the Pioneer Valley in 2025.

Federal prosecutors identified the defendant as Jacob D. Miller of Hadley. On Monday, Oct. 5, he pleaded guilty to charges involving unlawful importation of nuclear material, mailing hazardous materials, possession of ammunition and explosive materials as a convicted felon, and possession of child sexual abuse material. The [Justice Department’s Massachusetts office](https://www.justice.gov/usao-ma/pr/massachusetts-man-pleads-guilty-illegally-importing-and-selling-plutonium-russia) said U.S. District Court Judge Mark G. Mastroianni set sentencing for Jan. 21, 2027. A guilty plea resolves the charges, but sentencing has not yet occurred.

The case centers on an online business called Collect The Periodic Table, or CTPT. Prosecutors said Miller sold samples of chemical elements directly and through the Bonanza marketplace, operating the company from his residence in South Hadley. According to the federal account, the business was presented as a way to buy element samples, but the materials at issue included plutonium, which is highly radioactive, and thallium, which is highly toxic.

The Justice Department said Miller imported plutonium from Russia and arranged for it to be mailed to his home. From about Dec. 30, 2020, through March 31, 2025, prosecutors said he sold plutonium to approximately 67 customers in the United States and abroad, then shipped it from South Hadley through the U.S. mail even though the material was prohibited from being mailed. The department did not identify the customers or say in its announcement whether anyone was injured or exposed.

The same release said Miller sold thallium to about 71 customers between October 2017 and April 2025 and mailed that material in the same way. The [Boston Globe’s report](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/05/metro/hadley-russian-plutonium-thallium-online-sales/) added local background from earlier reporting, including that Massachusetts’ Radiation Control Program sent Miller a cease-and-desist letter in 2014 after learning he was selling depleted uranium on eBay. That earlier regulatory action is separate from the federal charges resolved by Monday’s plea.

Investigators searched Miller’s home in April 2025, according to prosecutors. They recovered bottles of explosive powder, ammunition and six rifles, which the Justice Department said he could not lawfully possess because of his prior felony convictions. Agents also found child sexual abuse material on his laptop and phone. Miller had been held in federal custody since his April 9, 2025, arrest, and a grand jury indicted him later that month, the department said.

The potential penalties vary by count. The nuclear-material importation charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, while the ammunition and explosive-material counts each carry up to 15 years. The mailing charge carries up to one year. Because prosecutors say Miller had a prior conviction for possessing child sexual abuse material, that count carries a statutory minimum of 10 years and a maximum of 20 years. Those figures are limits set by law, not a prediction of the sentence Judge Mastroianni will impose.

For the communities around Hadley and South Hadley, the case illustrates how a specialized online business can create public-safety and regulatory questions far beyond a single home. The public record now confirms the plea and the approximate number of customers identified by prosecutors, but it does not establish what happened to every shipment or whether any customer faces charges. The next major development will be the January sentencing hearing, where the court will weigh the applicable statutes, sentencing guidelines and the facts presented by both sides.
